doc.title: John Beal interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2024

title: Leonard Bernstein and conductors
summary: Beal praises Bernstein's pulse, recalls works played with him, and discusses distrust of conductors without a beat and Broadway pit conductors.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah, that’s great. That’s like a Bill Crow story. How about Leonard Bernstein?

Really he had the beat man. He had a great pulse. And he didn’t have to convey it, it was just there you know. It was there. And I played a couple of things with him. I played on a mass that he wrote, a recording, I played actually Fender bass on that. And there was a ballet piece he wrote called “Dybbuk” that I played on. And we did “Symphony of Psalms” at Carnegie Hall one time that he conducted. Really memorable, to me.
What kind of date or event tends to make you anxious or nervous? Is there anything that makes you apprehensive about it?
Well you’re always apprehensive playing a symphony concert, especially if you don’t trust the conductor. You know? That makes you apprehensive.
What wouldn’t you trust about a conductor? For cues or is it more than that?
No. I know one conductor who gives you a cue after you play, but —
In other words he heard it and goes, “Oh yes, thank you for coming in.”

I mean that’s being a little facetious you know but what I wouldn’t trust about a conductor is that the conductor doesn’t have the beat man, if he doesn’t have a good beat you know it’s a thing you have to — show a difference. A lot of orchestras are able to do that. They play together, you know, self-preservation. And mentioning Broadway, some of these conductors were rehearsal piano players and they learn the music and they get to conduct it and you know you shouldn’t follow them. And if a sub comes in and follows him he’s wrong because he’s not with the band, because the band knows better than to follow the conductor. I don’t want to get negative man.
Yeah. I understand what you’re saying. I’ve also, along the technology lines I’ve heard drummers talk about playing a Broadway show from another room.

Oh yeah. Yeah my friend Warren Odze, he was in another room, he was playing “Shrek.” You don’t even know who you’re playing with. And if you don’t have the mix in your phones you could be way off because you’re looking at the conductor. I had that happen to me.
